By incorporating a soft version of the DICE loss, SoftDICE can effectively handle distribution mismatch and improve the performance of imitation learning methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SoftDICE on several continuous control tasks and show that it outperforms existing methods in terms of both sample efficiency and performance. Additionally, SoftDICE can be easily combined with other methods, such as behavioral cloning and adversarial imitation learning, to further improve their performance. This term is derived from the Hessian eigenvalues of the generator's loss function, which are calculated using a specific method. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the Hessian eigenvalues and their relationship to mode collapse. Our findings are supported by empirical evidence from multiple GAN models and datasets. The code and data used in this research are available on GitHub. By doing so, we can ensure that the worst-performing function is not overly similar to the others, thereby preventing the collapse of performance. Our approach involves adding a penalty term to the Q-learning objective that encourages representation diversity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in both tabular and deep reinforcement learning settings, and show that it significantly improves the performance of ensemble Q-learning. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into the properties of the proposed objective and show that it is a generalization of existing ensemble Q-learning methods. Experimental results on various benchmark environments confirm that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both performance and representation diversity. Our findings suggest that targeting both routes with antiviral therapies may be necessary to effectively treat HCV infections. Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) is a distributed reinforcement learning technique that enables multiple agents to collaborate on a shared task without sharing their local data. FRL has been successfully applied in various domains, including robotics, autonomous driving, and recommender systems. Despite its potential, FRL faces several challenges, including communication limitations, data heterogeneity, and the need for robustness in dynamic environments. This survey aims to provide an in-depth examination of FRL, its applications, and the associated difficulties, as well as to identify promising research directions for future development. We begin by introducing the fundamental principles of FRL and its key components, followed by a comprehensive review of existing FRL methods. We then discuss the applications of FRL in multiple domains, highlighting its potential benefits and the associated challenges. Finally, we outline potential research directions for future FRL development. We hope that this survey will serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field of FRL. In semi-supervised learning, pseudo labeling is a common technique used to
expand the training set with unlabeled data. However, this approach can be
problematic when the model is initially weak, as it may assign incorrect
labels to the unlabeled data. To mitigate this issue, we propose a new
approach called Curriculum Pseudo Tagging (CPT), which involves assigning
labels to the unlabeled data in a way that prioritizes the most reliable
ones. Specifically, CPT assigns labels to the unlabeled data based on their
similarity to the labeled data, with the most similar data receiving the most
reliable labels. We also propose a new semi-supervised learning framework
called FlexMatch, which incorporates CPT to enhance the performance of
pretext-based models. The results of our experiments demonstrate that FlexMatch
outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets.

Data discretization is a crucial preprocessing step in machine learning, particularly for classification tasks. This paper presents a novel discretization approach, called Max-Relevance-Min-Divergence (MRMD), which balances data relevance and diversity. By maximizing the relevance of discretized data to the target variable and minimizing the divergence between discretized and original data, MRMD achieves effective data discretization. Experimental results demonstrate that MRMD outperforms existing methods in terms of classification accuracy, particularly when used with Naive Bayes classifiers. Additionally, MRMD's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyinwang/MRMD. Experimental results show that MRMD-MD achieves comparable performance to MRMD on complete datasets and significantly outperforms other methods on datasets with missing data. The source code for MRMD-MD is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyinwang/MRMD-MD. The CORSIKA 8 air shower simulation code has undergone significant development, 
enabling researchers to study extensive air showers with enhanced precision. 
This presentation highlights the key advancements made to CORSIKA 8, including 
the incorporation of new hadronic interaction models, improved particle 
detection capabilities, and the integration of multiple air shower observatories. 
Additionally, the presentation showcases the code's potential for simulating 
neutrino-induced events and the detection of cosmic rays by future observatories. 
CORSIKA 8's capabilities are further demonstrated through the simulation of 
extensive air showers at the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Cherenkov Telescope 
Array. The presentation also explores the code's potential for simulating 
future observatories, including the Southern Ocean and the Giant Radio Array. 
Finally, the presentation highlights the code's contributions to the development 
of the next-generation air shower simulation code, CoREAS.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has been successfully applied to numerous real-world tasks, yet its practical applications are often hindered by the need for extensive data collection and the potential for agents to become stuck in suboptimal states. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach, temporal change reinforcement learning (TCRL), which enables RL agents to adapt to changing environments by leveraging temporal information. This approach is demonstrated through the application of TCRL to the challenging domain of robotic manipulation, where agents must learn to adapt to changing object properties. Experimental results show that TCRL outperforms traditional RL methods in terms of sample efficiency and task completion rates. Furthermore, we examine the impact of incorporating temporal information on the agent's decision-making process and find that TCRL agents tend to focus on the most relevant features of the environment, leading to more efficient and effective learning outcomes. The accompanying video provides a visual representation of the TCRL approach in action. As the demand for edge computing continues to rise, there is a growing need for efficient deep neural network (DNN) accelerators that minimize energy consumption. To address this challenge, we introduce ENOS, a novel framework for designing hybrid DNN accelerators that combine digital and compute-in-memory (CIM) components. ENOS employs a genetic algorithm to optimize the placement of CIM layers within a digital accelerator, resulting in significant energy savings. Our framework is capable of adapting to various DNN models, accelerator architectures, and energy constraints, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by designing an ENOS-based accelerator for the ResNet-18 model. Our results show that the proposed accelerator achieves a 2.5x reduction in energy consumption compared to a traditional digital-only accelerator, and a 1.5x improvement over a previous state-of-the-art hybrid accelerator. Furthermore, ENOS can be easily extended to accommodate additional requirements, such as latency constraints, by incorporating a multi-objective optimization approach. Our findings highlight the potential of ENOS as a powerful tool for designing energy-efficient hybrid DNN accelerators. The source code for ENOS is available on GitHub.

We investigate the structure of cyclic groups of prime order, with their Hodge series sharing the same characteristics as that of the cyclic group of prime order $p$. This investigation leads to the conclusion that the cyclic group of prime order $p$ is the sole non-abelian example of this class, with all other instances being abelian and having a relatively small order. Furthermore, we derive a formula to calculate the order of these abelian groups. Additionally, we examine the structure of the cyclic group of prime order $p$ when its Hodge series exhibits a specific pattern, with $p$ being a square-free number. The widespread dissemination of polarizing content on social media platforms has been linked to a rise in societal divisions. To counteract this trend, we've developed an algorithm that aims to reduce the visibility of polarizing content on these platforms. Our approach involves creating a model that simulates the spread of polarizing opinions within a network, where users are exposed to opposing views at a rate determined by the algorithm. By optimizing the algorithm's parameters, we can minimize the number of users holding unfavorable opinions. Our results show that this algorithm can effectively reduce the visibility of polarizing content, even when users are initially biased towards extreme views. Furthermore, we've identified a phenomenon where the algorithm's effectiveness can be hindered by a 'backfire effect', where users who are initially exposed to opposing views may become more entrenched in their original opinions. To mitigate this effect, we've developed a modified algorithm that incorporates a 'backfire penalty' to account for this phenomenon. Our findings suggest that this algorithm can be an effective tool for social media platforms seeking to reduce the visibility of polarizing content.
